Replacing pointwise BCE loss with pairwise BPR loss (sampling within-user positive-negative pairs) will improve GAUC and nDCG@5 because it directly optimizes within-user ranking rather than absolute score calibration
mechanism: GAUC is per-user AUC which counts correct pairwise orderings within each user's impression list. BPR directly maximizes the probability that positive items are ranked above negative items for the same user, which is exactly the quantity GAUC measures. With only ~5 impressions per user in validation, each pairwise ordering matters enormously. BCE optimizes marginal scores independently and may not produce the correct within-user ordering even when item-level calibration is good.

evidence.task_structure: Validation has ~5 rows/user; GAUC = per-user AUC = fraction of (pos, neg) pairs correctly ordered within same user. With 5 items, there are at most 6 such pairs. BPR directly maximizes these. BCE has no such guarantee.
evidence.previous_experiments: Node 0 shows train_primary=0.6918 vs val_primary=0.6015 — large gap suggesting the model overfits to absolute score calibration rather than within-user ordering. BPR's relative objective may generalize better.
evidence.literature: W2539247542 (LambdaFM) shows FM + pairwise ranking loss outperforms FM + pointwise loss for implicit feedback recommendation, specifically for ranking metrics like AUC and nDCG.

proposed_change: Replace the pointwise BCE training loop with a BPR pairwise loss: for each minibatch, sample (user, pos_item, neg_item) triples where both pos and neg come from the same user's training data, compute score difference, and optimize with -log(sigmoid(s_pos - s_neg)). Keep the same FM architecture, embedding dim k=16, Adam optimizer.
expected_result: Improvement of 0.003-0.010 in val_primary, mainly through GAUC improvement since BPR directly optimizes pairwise ordering
falsification_condition: If val_primary does not improve by more than 0.002 over the 0.6015 baseline, the hypothesis is wrong — either the FM embeddings already capture within-user ordering well enough with BCE, or the training distribution mismatch (train ~44 rows/user vs valid ~5 rows/user) negates the benefit

Combined with the existing video-level features in the FM, the model gets two complementary quality signals at different granularities.

evidence.task_structure: 18291/22377 valid users have varying author_id in their impression list, meaning author-level features can discriminate within the evaluation set. Authors have many more impressions than individual videos (7583 videos vs 3+ authors per video), so per-author rates are more statistically reliable.
evidence.previous_experiments: Node 6 showed video-level pos_rate+log_count improved over baseline by +0.0004. Node 11 tried user-author affinity (two features: user-author pair rate + author rate) and got 0.5854 - but this combined noisy user-author pairs with author rates. A clean per-author rate alone (analogous to node 6) hasn't been tried.

proposed_change: Starting from node 6 code, add two more features: per-author positive rate (quantile-bucketed into 10 bins + 1 UNK) and per-author log10 impression count from training data, computed from train rows only. This extends the FM input from 7 fields to 9 fields.
expected_result: Improvement of 0.002-0.004 over baseline (0.6039-0.6059 val primary), similar to or better than node 6's gain, since author-level signals are more reliable than video-level signals.
falsification_condition: If val primary stays below 0.6021 (within noise of node 6's 0.6019), the hypothesis is wrong - author-level quality signals either don't add new information beyond video-level signals or the FM can't effectively use them.

risks.leakage: Author stats computed strictly from training rows only (before validation dates), same as node 6's approach. No leakage.
risks.overfitting: Adding 2 more embedding rows (22 extra parameters each with k=16) is negligible relative to 1.14M training rows. No overfitting risk.
risks.runtime: Negligible additional computation - O(N) pass over training rows to compute author stats. Runtime stays well under 15 minutes.

candidates_considered: Per-author positive rate + log_count features (analogous to node 6's video-level features but at author granularity, which aggregates more observations and has 18291/22377 users with varying author_id in valid)
Hybrid FM + continuous video pos_rate as direct linear score term rather than bucketed embedding, which might generalize better by avoiding quantile bucket boundary noise
Duration-ratio feature: per-video quantile of play_time_ms/duration_ms (completion rate proxy) as a cleaner behavioral signal than raw play_time
reflection: Node 14 (listwise softmax) scored 0.6017, within noise of best 0.6019. All modifications to node 6 have failed or been within noise floor. The video pos_rate + log_count features (node 6) remain the best. I've tried: user-author affinity (bad), video-tab interaction (bad), click rate (bad), completion rate (bad), video category (bad), listwise loss (noise), BPR loss (bad). I have not tried a clean per-author positive rate as a standalone feature analogous to node 6's video-level rate.

hypothesis: Adding a user-tag affinity feature (per-(user_id, primary_tag) historical positive rate from training, bucketed) will improve ranking by capturing within-user variation in content preference
mechanism: Within each user's 5-impression candidate set, videos differ by their tag (content category from video_features_basic_pure.csv). A user who historically preferred tag X will have a higher affinity score for videos with tag X vs tag Y. This varies within the candidate set and thus contributes to ranking contrast — unlike user-side features that are constant per user. The FM can use this as a direct preference signal that personalizes ranking beyond global item popularity.

evidence.task_structure: With ~5 candidates per user, only within-user-varying features matter. Tags in video_features_basic_pure.csv are multi-valued but the primary (first) tag is a compact categorical. Training has ~44 rows/user so user-tag affinity estimates are feasible for frequent users.
evidence.previous_experiments: Node 11 tried user-author affinity and scored 0.5854 (worse), but author space is very sparse (too many distinct authors for reliable estimates). Tag space is much smaller, making affinity estimates more reliable. Node 6 showed video-level pos_rate helps (+0.003 over baseline), suggesting engagement statistics are useful — the question is whether personalizing them to user level adds more.

proposed_change: Load video_features_basic_pure.csv to get tag→primary_tag map. Compute per-(user_id, primary_tag) positive rate from training rows. Quantile-bucket into 10 bins + 1 UNK. Add as a 10th feature column to the FM input (offset from dim_extended). Keep all other features from node 15.
expected_result: Gain of +0.003 to +0.006 on validation primary, similar to how video pos_rate helped in node 6, but more personalized. If the tag space is too sparse per user, the gain may be smaller (~0.001-0.002).
falsification_condition: If validation primary does not exceed 0.6024 (current best + noise floor), the hypothesis is wrong — user-tag affinity from training is too sparse or the tag feature doesn't discriminate within-user candidate sets enough.

risks.leakage: Low — affinity is computed from training rows only, which are strictly before validation/test dates
risks.overfitting: Medium — user-tag affinity is a sparse feature (many (user,tag) pairs appear only 1-2 times in training), may overfit to noise; mitigated by bucketing which groups similar values
risks.runtime: Low — reading video_features_basic_pure.csv is fast (small file already used), affinity computation is O(train_rows)

candidates_considered: User-tag affinity: compute per-(user,tag) historical positive rate from training, add as FM feature — within-user-varying personalization signal, tag space is compact enough for reliable estimates
User-tab affinity: compute per-(user,tab) historical positive rate, but tab is already directly embedded in the FM so this is mostly redundant
Temporal recency weighting for video stats: exponentially decay old training impressions — refines item-side signal but adds no personalization
reflection: Node 15 added author-level pos_rate and log_count features but only gained +0.0006 which is below the noise floor (0.0008 std). The spread [0.6018,0.6024,0.6023] barely exceeds baseline. Author-side popularity statistics don't add enough personalization. The FM already embeds author_id directly, so the bucket features are redundant with what embeddings already capture.

hypothesis: Adding an explicit (dur_bucket, tab) cross-feature as a new FM field will improve ranking by providing a direct encoding of context-specific item quality that the FM cross terms cannot fully capture, especially for users who see items across different tabs with different durations.
mechanism: GAUC and nDCG@5 depend on correctly ordering items within a user's ~5-impression candidate set. Tab varies for 40% of users and dur_bucket varies for 70%. The joint (dur_bucket, tab) combination has ~150 possible values, well-covered in training, and its embedding directly captures 'short video in recommendation tab' vs 'long video in search tab' quality differences. The FM's implicit cross term (dur_bucket × tab) is learned through shared embeddings and may not fully capture this interaction; an explicit combined feature adds a dedicated embedding.

evidence.task_structure: tab=0 has 3.5% long_view rate while tab=4 has 45.9% — huge tab effect. Duration also varies (pos videos avg 99K ms vs neg 104K ms). Their interaction encodes meaningful context. 8917/22377 users see items across multiple tabs, and 15656/22377 see items with varying dur_bucket.
evidence.previous_experiments: Node 15 (best=0.6022) shows item-side quality features help. Node 9 showed category ID alone didn't help much. Node 12 showed (video,tab) joint pos_rate was too sparse and hurt. Explicit cross-feature embedding with only 150 values should avoid sparsity issues.

proposed_change: In the feature engineering section of node 15's code, add a new field: (dur_bucket_index * 20 + tab_as_int) combined ID, offset into the embedding table as a new field with ~150 valid values + 1 UNK. This creates one new feature column per row derived entirely from existing fields, no new data needed.
expected_result: Modest improvement of +0.002 to +0.004 over node 15's 0.6022, bringing validation primary to ~0.6024-0.6062. If the cross-feature doesn't add information beyond what FM already captures implicitly, the score will remain near 0.6022.
falsification_condition: Validation primary stays at or below 0.6022, or drops significantly (>0.002 below) indicating the extra parameter overhead hurts more than the new signal helps.

risks.leakage: None — dur_bucket and tab are both present at inference time as raw features of the impression being scored, no historical aggregation needed.
risks.overfitting: Low — only ~150 combinations, well-covered in 1.14M training rows. Each combination will have thousands of training examples.
risks.runtime: Negligible — just one extra integer column computed from two existing fields.

candidates_considered: Add per-video mean completion ratio (play_time_ms/duration_ms) from raw training CSV, quantile-bucketed, as a 10th feature on top of node 15's 9 fields — marginal gain expected since video_pos_rate already encodes much of this.
Add per-(user, first_level_category) positive rate from training (38 categories × 26K users) as user-category affinity — less sparse than per-(user,tag) but same overfitting risk shown in node 16.

Add (dur_bucket × tab) explicit cross-feature as a new FM field — only ~150 combinations, well-covered in training, captures context-specific duration preferences that vary within user candidate sets.
reflection: Node 16 added per-(user,tag) affinity features and massively overfit (train 0.8184, val 0.5693). This rules out sparse user-specific historical features. Node 15 (best=0.6022) uses FM with 9 fields: base 5 + video_pos_rate + video_log_count + author_pos_rate + author_log_count. The gap from baseline (0.6022 vs 0.6016) is small but consistent. We need a different type of signal — not more user-level personalization but better item-side context modeling.
